terra.problem: The passage does not say Judah was supposed to improve with every generation.
Imitating all the nations’ abominations does not establish that their worship was identical in every respect.
The passage does not say these practices were why the nations were driven out.
The text does not mention captives, but it does not establish that Shishak took no people.
The claim that nobody would mistake the bronze shields for the originals adds an unmarked claim about what people would recognize.
The passage does not say Rehoboam had nothing left to work with or that this was why he made bronze shields.
The war lasted throughout the kings’ days; saying the kingdoms never turned to peace goes beyond that period.
The text says the war lasted throughout their days, not that it lasted through the entirety of both kings’ reigns.
Being buried with his fathers in the City of David does not establish that Rehoboam was buried in a family plot.
The text says Abijam’s heart was not as fully devoted as David’s; it does not simply say it was not fully devoted.
The text does not say there was no idol removal during Abijam’s reign.
The explanation is generic and ends by repeating the answer without adding a distinctive Papa Dorin observation.
The text says the LORD acted for David’s sake; it does not say Abijam had not earned the lamp.
Saying Asa kept his own place with the LORD instead adds a contrast the passage does not make about his action.
The text says Abijam’s heart was not as fully devoted as David’s, not simply that it was not fully devoted.
Baasha fortified Ramah to prevent movement into or out of Asa’s territory. The text does not describe a roadblock across the whole territory.
The text says Baasha fortified Ramah, not that he built a wall.
The aside about nobody enjoying taxes is a generic observation rather than a clear joke, and the rest repeats the answer.
Referring to the next card talks about the lesson’s presentation, which Papa Dorin does not do.
The text does not say Asa intended to leave Baasha alone with his problem.
Asa asks Ben-hadad to break his treaty with Baasha; the message does not say he is to attack Baasha.
The text gives Asa’s request, but does not establish that he was not looking for a peacemaker.
The text says Ben-hadad listened and sent his commanders against Israel’s cities. It does not explicitly say he accepted the gift.
The passage does not explicitly say Ben-hadad accepted the gift or broke the treaty, even though he listened to Asa and attacked Israel’s cities.
Calling the fortification no longer Baasha’s biggest problem assigns him a priority the text does not state.
The text does not say Ramah was half built; it says Baasha stopped fortifying it.
Asa summoned all the men of Judah, not every person in Judah. The text also does not explicitly say they dismantled completed work.
The passage does not say Baasha was no longer in charge at Ramah or identify the building work as a wall.
The text does not say that nothing went to waste.
The text says Asa became diseased in his feet in old age; it does not say age caused the disease.
Saying the disease came after forty-one years on the throne places it after his reign. The text says only that it came in his old age.
The explanation is generic: it rules out the choice, repeats the answer, and tells the baker to remember it without adding an observation.
